newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT - Swimming looks to cash in on Loader.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT - Swimming looks to cash in on Loader.

text.p: CHRISTCHURCH, Sept 5 - Swimming New Zealand will take its first step this month towards capitalising on Danyon Loader's Olympic gold medals, NZPA reports.

A meeting in Rotorua on September 17, the eve of the two-day national winter championships, will discuss ways for the sport to cash in on the phenomenal interest created by Loader's Atlanta successes.

Loader's coach Duncan Laing said today New Zealand swimming must not waste the opportunity and he plans to file a report at the meeting outlining ways to make the most out of Loader's Olympic 200m and 400m freestyle gold medal achievements.
Those medals gave swimming the biggest lift that probably any New Zealand sport has seen since track star Peter Snell's double gold success 32 years ago.
Laing is determined not to let his sport slide down hill, as happened to hockey after winning gold at Montreal in 1976, and with soccer after making the World Cup finals in 1982.
He said he had several ideas which would be put forward at the Atlanta debriefing meeting in Rotorua in 12 days' time.
These included the setting up of fulltime regional swimming camps, full financial support for touring New Zealand development squads and Loader's support appearance at training camps.

"We might have to look at the coaches as well. We have a lot of good kids swimming in the country areas. But it's no good bringing those swimmers to camps for 14 days and then sending them home if the coach hasn't got the facilities or the know-how to keep that child going," Laing said.
"But overall we as a country have got to use Danyon's great swims in Atlanta to boost swimming and get parents behind the sport."
Laing has been a driving force behind New Zealand swimming for years and Loader said at Atlanta the Dunedin coach was just hitting his prime.
The coach has visions of swimming rising up to become a leading summer sport in New Zealand.
The hurdles until now had been lack of profile, which Loader resolved in Atlanta, and a lack of money.
"I'm hoping the new man in charge of New Zealand swimming, Bruce Smith, will be a livewire who could secure major sponsorship for the sport," Laing said.
"We can't just sit around and wait for money from the Sports Foundation."
Smith, swimming's new executive director, begins his new job in Wellington tomorrow.
Laing said big international sponsors could see the benefit in making mileage out of Loader and swimming. Until now though, swimming had battled through a rough course.
"If an All Black attends a training camp they get all the gear, tracksuit, bag, maybe a pair of boots and top accommodation. It would be nice if our squad could get the same opportunity.
"Until now, swimmers have gone away, sleeping in poor accommodation, sometimes on the floor, and they haven't been given any uniform because there's no money. What incentive is there in that?
"If all that changes and they go away, stay in a decent place, get some decent gear, then they are going to want to train and continue representing New Zealand."
Meanwhile, Laing said there was life for Loader after the Olympics and a group of Dunedin business people had offered to pay for the champion's education.
"I think he might be staying here, instead of having to go to university in the United States. We haven't discussed that with Danyon yet."
Loader is on holiday in the United States and will return home in a fortnight. He wants a university degree but has had difficulty fitting in lectures at Otago and doing his training.
"I am sure he could train for three sessions a week in between his university work -- then he's got the whole weekend for training. He's very keen to carry on in swimming.

"But a company is flying him to Japan to do some work with some children. So if he's going to work with Japanese children he's bound to be wanting to work with New Zealanders. He's keen on that sort of thing," Laing said.
